question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old woman arrived to the rheumatology infusion suite this morning at the request of her primary physician to review persistent polyarticular pain, confirm baseline organ status, and discuss escalation from weekly subcutaneous methotrexate to a biologic agent if warranted. She recalls that aching and morning stiffness in the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and knees began at age 33, at which time serologies revealed a rheumatoid factor of 132 IU/mL and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies of 86 U/mL; radiographs two years later showed marginal erosions at the second proximal interphalangeal joints. Over the past decade she has managed fatigue, episodic low-grade fevers, and symmetric synovitis with a combination of methotrexate 20 mg weekly, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, and low-dose folic acid, supplemented twice yearly with intramuscular methylprednisolone when flares limited her ability to type at work. She denies sicca symptoms, malar rash, photosensitive eruptions, or serositis, and there has been no history of interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, or exertional dyspnea; she jogs three miles three times weekly without wheeze or prolonged cough and has never carried an inhaler. Five years ago she was admitted overnight for coffee-ground emesis after a week of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use during a hand-swelling flare; esophagogastroduodenoscopy at that time demonstrated a 1.5-cm posterior duodenal ulcer with a clean base and negative rapid urease test. She completed a two-week course of amoxicillin, clarithromycin, and omeprazole for empiric Helicobacter eradication, and since then remains on pantoprazole 40 mg each morning; she reports no subsequent dyspepsia, melena, or iron-deficiency anemia. Endocrine review reveals that a routine employment screening six years ago uncovered a fasting plasma glucose of 152 mg/dL; she initiated lifestyle modification and later began metformin extended-release 1 g nightly. Finger-stick readings at home typically range 110–160 mg/dL, her last glycated hemoglobin measured two months ago was 7.1 %, and she has never experienced blurred vision, paresthesias, pedal ulcers, proteinuria, or ketoacidosis. Cardiovascular history is unremarkable: she comfortably climbs four flights of stairs to her office, has never had chest pressure, diaphoresis, left-arm radiation, or emergency evaluation for suspected infarction, and her most recent exercise treadmill study performed before marathon training last year was negative for ischemia. Blood pressure has been stable near 118/72 mm Hg without antihypertensives, and lipid profile last week showed total cholesterol 182 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL, HDL 58 mg/dL, and triglycerides 122 mg/dL. She denies intermittent claudication, toe discoloration, or non-healing wounds, and ankle pulses have remained full and symmetric on routine examinations. Neurologic inquiry brings no episodes of sudden speech disturbance, unilateral weakness, facial droop, or gait imbalance; she continues to perform complex spreadsheet analysis at work, balances household finances, and has had no memory lapses reported by family. She drinks one glass of wine on Friday evenings, abstains from tobacco and illicit drugs, and has received three previous negative HIV tests as part of infertility evaluations. Family history includes a mother with hypothyroidism and a father who underwent cholecystectomy; no early coronary disease, stroke, or malignancy is noted among first-degree relatives. Current medications, in addition to those mentioned, include calcium 600 mg with vitamin D₃ 800 IU twice daily and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for headaches; she does not take biologics, anticoagulants, or herbal supplements. On examination today she is alert, appropriately groomed, and in no acute distress with a body-mass index of 27 kg/m². Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 120/74 mm Hg seated in the left arm, heart rate 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. Hands reveal mild ulnar deviation, fusiform swelling of the second through fourth proximal interphalangeal joints bilaterally, and a tender, boggy right wrist; elbow and shoulder motion are full without effusion. No jugular venous distention is visible; S1 and S2 are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout, and diaphragmatic excursion is intact. Abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds; there is no epigastric tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses, and the liver edge is not appreciated. Distal pulses are 2 + at the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, and there is no edema, cyanosis, or skin ulceration. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, and symmetric sensation to light touch and vibration in all extremities. Laboratories drawn this morning reveal hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white-cell count 6.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets 314 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (estimated glomerular filtration rate 98 mL/min/1.73 m²), fasting glucose 156 mg/dL, HbA1c as noted 7.1 %, AST 26 U/L, ALT 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 78 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.4 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.0. Urinalysis is negative for protein, blood, and ketones. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, axis within normal limits, and no Q waves or ST-segment abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the hands confirm mild progression of juxta-articular osteopenia and small erosions without new joint-space narrowing. She seeks counsel on risks and benefits of adding a tumor-necrosis-factor inhibitor, strategies to minimize gastrointestinal relapse given her prior ulcer, and guidance on maintaining glycemic control while her physical activity fluctuates with joint inflammation.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index sums weights for qualifying baseline conditions. Age adjustment adds no points before age 50.
- Rheumatic disease: seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis → 1.
- Peptic ulcer disease: prior endoscopically confirmed duodenal ulcer → 1. Its bleeding presentation does not add another point.
- Diabetes without end-organ damage: metformin-treated type 2 diabetes with no documented nephropathy, neuropathy, or retinopathy → 1, rather than 2 for complicated diabetes.
- Age 47 → 0.
- Other CCI conditions: no documented MI, heart failure, peripheral vascular or cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic lung disease, liver disease, significant renal disease, hemiplegia, malignancy, or AIDS → 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
